results.corrected_extracted: Seven consumer drug-checking services in the TEDI project analysed 45,859 samples handed in voluntarily in 2008–2013: DIMS (Netherlands) 28,613, Energy Control (Spain) 8,305, Ailaket (Basque country) 1,629, Saferparty (Switzerland) 3,290, Checkit! (Austria) 3,078, Modus Fiesta (Belgium, from 2011) 244 and Check!n (Portugal, three editions of one festival) 700. The text says the Netherlands received mostly ecstasy tablets; in Figure 1 they are its largest sample type, about 45% of DIMS samples (approximate reading). The Basque country and Portugal received no ecstasy tablets; Spain and Austria received more MDMA crystals than tablets. Figure 1 shows each service's mix of four drug types only as percentages of its total; no sample numbers are given by year or drug type.
results.note: Counts match the Figure 1 labels and sum to 45,859. But Figure 1 shows ecstasy pills at about 45% of DIMS samples (largest type, not a majority), and it does give each service's type mix, as percentages.

My 300-dpi readings: 2009 Austria 18.5, Spain 30.8, Switzerland 46.7, Netherlands 63.6; 2013 Spain 62.1, Austria 78.0, Netherlands 91.7, Switzerland 95.2, Belgium 100. Spain is about 1 point higher using triangle box centres; within reading error.

My readings: 2009 Netherlands 62, Spain 65, Switzerland 70, Austria 74; 2013 Spain 104, Austria 107, Switzerland 113, Netherlands 114; Austria 2010 43. Ratios 1.84 and 1.44-1.62 confirm. The text's ranges omit Austria 2009 and Spain 2013.

Table 2 (PDF p. 8) and Results (PDF p. 5) match cell by cell: mCPP in all five for 2008; DXM at Ailaket, Energy Control, Netherlands; 4-MEC at Austria, Energy Control, Switzerland. Table gives no counts.

results.corrected_extracted: For each tablet, logo, diameter, thickness, weight, colour and groove were recorded; a tablet from a batch already analysed by GC-MS at least three times was taken as identified by its colour-test result and these features, and the person who brought it was given the batch's average content and range. The authors state that this recognition has proven very reliable in the Netherlands, citing earlier work, with no data in this paper, and do not say whether such tablets are counted in the figures. Limits they state: people using the services do not necessarily represent all people who use drugs (they add that earlier comparisons found people who used testing broadly similar to those who did not); the services differed greatly in scale; an unknown proportion of people are not interested in testing; laboratories analysed substances as salt or as base, which was taken into account but might still have affected some purity results; and techniques differed in sensitivity, and possibly in how up to date their spectral libraries were, which could have led to underreporting of new substances and adulterants.
results.note: Salt-or-base reporting is tied in the source to purity results, not to underreporting, which it links to sensitivity and libraries. The authors' counterpoint (testers broadly similar to non-testers) was omitted.

reporting_issues.correction: issue: Sample sizes are given only per service for the whole period (Figure 1 labels); Figure 1 shows each service's mix of four drug types only as percentage bars summing to 100%, so it is unclear whether the 45,859 samples include other drugs; no numbers are given by year or by drug type, and there are no intervals. | consequence: Yearly percentages from small services (for example Belgium) may rest on few samples; their precision cannot be judged.

issue: Whether tablets identified by logo, physical features and colour test, without new laboratory analysis, were counted in the results, and with what values (the batch average given to the person who brought the tablet), is not stated; the paper describes the procedure for the testing facilities in general, without saying which services used it, and claims its reliability for the Netherlands (PDF p. 2). | consequence: If included, such tablets would repeat earlier batch results and hide any variation within a logo; the paper gives no basis for claims about logos.
